current: Numbers opens in the wilderness of Sinai on the first day of the second month of the second year — the Torah is suddenly precise about its chronology, as if the nation has moved from mythic time into historical time.
problem: The Torah is not suddenly precise here: Exodus already dates events to the day (e.g. the Tabernacle set up on the first day of the first month of the second year). Calling the earlier narrative 'mythic time' is an editorial judgment the text does not make.
evidence: Exodus 40:17 (JPS): 'In the first month of the second year, on the first of the month, the Tabernacle was set up.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Exodus.40.17 ; Numbers 1:1: 'On the first day of the second month, in the second year after the exodus from the land of Egypt, GOD spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.1.1
fix: Numbers opens in the wilderness of Sinai on the first day of the second month of the second year after the Exodus, one month after the Tabernacle was set up (Numbers 1:1; Exodus 40:17).

current: The results are tabulated: Reuben, Simeon, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, Dan, Asher, Gad, Naphtali — 603,550 men of fighting age, not counting the Levites who are exempt from military service because they serve the Tabernacle.
problem: This is the order of the tribal leaders list (1:5-15), not the order in which the results are tabulated. In the tally (1:20-43) Gad comes third, after Simeon and before Judah.
evidence: Numbers 1:20-26 (JPS): 'those enrolled from the tribe of Reuben: 46,500 ... Simeon: 59,300 ... Of the descendants of Gad ... 45,650. Of the descendants of Judah ... 74,600' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.1.20-43 ; Numbers 1:49-50: 'Do not on any account enroll the tribe of Levi ... You shall put the Levites in charge of the Tabernacle' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.1.47-50
fix: The results are tabulated: Reuben, Simeon, Gad, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Ephraim, Manasseh, Benjamin, Dan, Asher, Naphtali — 603,550 men of fighting age, not counting the Levites, who are not enrolled with the other tribes because they are put in charge of the Tabernacle.

current: Judah leads the east side, the place of honor and first march.
problem: The text calls the east side 'the front' and says Judah's division marches first; it does not call it the place of honor.
evidence: Numbers 2:3 (JPS): 'Camped on the front, or east side: the standard of the division of Judah'; 2:9: 'These shall march first.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.2.3 ; https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.2.9
fix: Judah leads the east side, which the Torah calls the front, and marches first (Numbers 2:3, 2:9).

current: If taken literally, the Sinai peninsula could not have supported such a population.
problem: A scholarly judgment stated as settled fact; the Torah itself says the people were fed by manna. It should be attributed to scholars.
evidence: Wikipedia, The Exodus: the 603,550 figure implies a population that would be 'far more than could be supported by the Sinai Desert' (scholarly view) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Exodus
fix: Many scholars argue that the Sinai desert could not naturally have supported such a population.

current: This ambivalence explains why the census in Numbers is conducted via a half-shekel coin per person rather than a direct headcount: the coins are counted rather than people themselves.
problem: Numbers 1 never mentions coins; the half-shekel census is commanded in Exodus 30:12-13. That the Numbers census was taken through half-shekels is Ramban's reading, not stated fact.
evidence: Ramban on Numbers 1:3: 'he [Moses] was not to count them [by persons] but that they were each to give half a shekel as a ransom for their soul (Exodus 30:12-13) ... and thereby know the number of the people.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Ramban_on_Numbers.1.3 ; Numbers 1:2-3 contains no mention of coins https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.1.1
fix: The Torah does not say how the census in Numbers was taken, but Ramban (on Numbers 1:3) says it was done through half-shekels, as in Exodus 30:12-13, so that the coins were counted rather than the people themselves.

current: The command to count Israelites 'by their hosts' is read by Rashi as indicating that God loves Israel so much that God counts them constantly — but the mechanism of indirect counting (through coins or other proxies) becomes a standard principle in Jewish law.
problem: Rashi's comment about God's love is on Numbers 1:1 (the opening verse), not on the words 'by their hosts'.
evidence: Rashi on Numbers 1:1: 'מִתּוֹךְ חִבָּתָן לְפָנָיו מוֹנֶה אוֹתָם כָּל שָׁעָה' ('Because they were dear to him, He counts them every now and then') https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Rashi_on_Numbers.1.1 ; Yoma 22b: 'Rabbi Yitzḥak said: It is prohibited to count Jews directly, even for the purposes of a mitzva' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Yoma.22b
fix: Rashi on Numbers 1:1 says God counts Israel often because they are dear to Him, and the Talmud (Yoma 22b) teaches that it is forbidden to count Jews directly, so counting through proxies became the rule in Jewish law.

current: Egyptian, Mesopotamian, and Hittite records all include population counts and military rosters.
problem: Only the Mesopotamian (Mari) census parallel was found in a source; the Egyptian and Hittite claims were not supported.
evidence: Encyclopedia.com, Mari: 'The Mari authorities used periodic censuses of tribes ... The purpose of the census seems to have been military conscription, taxation, and land distribution' https://www.encyclopedia.com/places/commonwealth-independent-states-and-baltic-nations/cis-and-baltic-political-geography/mari
fix: Records from Mari in Mesopotamia describe periodic censuses of tribes, taken for military conscription, taxation and land distribution.

current: The tribal organization described in Numbers — with each tribe occupying a designated quadrant around a central sacred space — mirrors the layout of Egyptian military camps, which were organized with the pharaoh's tent in the center and contingents arranged by position of honor around it.
problem: A scholarly proposal (Michael Homan, comparing Ramesses II's camp at Kadesh) stated as fact; Homan's parallel concerns the Tabernacle's plan and the pharaoh's central tent, and no source was found for contingents 'arranged by position of honor'.
evidence: Summary of Homan, 'The Divine Warrior in His Tent' (Bible Review): Ramesses' camp is 'rectangular ... At the center of the camp is a rectangular tent'; 'For Homan the plan and layout of the Tabernacle reflects those of Egyptian military camps' https://library.biblicalarchaeology.org/article/the-divine-warrior-in-his-tent/ ; https://www.templestudies.org/review-of-homan-michael-m-the-divine-warrior-in-his-tent-a-military-model-for-yahwehs-tabernacle/
fix: Some scholars, such as Michael Homan, compare the Tabernacle at the center of the camp to Egyptian military camps like that of Ramesses II at Kadesh, which had the pharaoh's tent at its center.

current: Then a series of laws address conditions that require leaving the camp — anyone with tzara'at or a bodily discharge — maintaining the holiness of the Israelite camp as a divine dwelling.
problem: Incomplete list: the verse also sends out anyone defiled by a corpse.
evidence: Numbers 5:2 (JPS): 'remove from camp anyone with an eruption or a discharge and anyone defiled by a corpse.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.5.2
fix: Then a series of laws address conditions that require leaving the camp — anyone with tzara'at, a bodily discharge, or impurity from a corpse — maintaining the holiness of the Israelite camp as a divine dwelling.

current: The Sotah ritual — one of the Torah's most controversial passages — addresses jealousy within marriage: a husband who suspects his wife of infidelity may bring her before the priest, who administers a water ordeal involving sacred ink dissolved in the water; if she is guilty, the water causes physical harm; if innocent, she is cleared and the Torah says she will conceive.
problem: The Torah does not call the ink sacred. It is the water that is 'sacral/holy water', mixed with earth from the Tabernacle floor, and the written curses are rubbed off into it.
evidence: Numbers 5:17 (JPS): 'The priest shall take sacral water in an earthen vessel and, taking some of the earth that is on the floor of the Tabernacle, the priest shall put it into the water'; 5:23: 'The priest shall put these curses down in writing and r[ub it off into the water]' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.5.17-23
fix: The Sotah ritual — one of the Torah's most controversial passages — addresses jealousy within marriage: a husband who suspects his wife of infidelity may bring her before the priest, who has her drink holy water mixed with dust from the Tabernacle floor and with written curses rubbed off into it; if she is guilty, the water causes physical harm; if innocent, she is cleared and the Torah says she will conceive.

current: The Priestly Blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) is the oldest text in the Hebrew Bible for which we have physical archaeological evidence: two tiny silver scrolls discovered in 1979 at Ketef Hinnom near Jerusalem, dating to the late 7th century BCE (roughly 2,600 years ago), contain these exact words.
problem: The scrolls do not contain 'these exact words': they preserve a shorter, partly broken version of the blessing. Their date is given as late 7th or early 6th century BCE.
evidence: Wikipedia, Ketef Hinnom scrolls: KH2 has 'only the bold italicized portion' of the blessing; 'all of Numbers 6:25–26 may have appeared on KH1 ... where the scroll has disintegrated'; dated c. 650–587 BCE, 'immediately prior to the destruction of Jerusalem' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ketef_Hinnom_scrolls
fix: The Priestly Blessing (Numbers 6:24–26) appears in the oldest surviving texts known from the Hebrew Bible: two tiny silver scrolls discovered in 1979 at Ketef Hinnom near Jerusalem, dated to the late 7th or early 6th century BCE, carry a shorter version of the blessing.

current: The Priestly Blessing is recited by kohanim (priestly descendants) in every synagogue service worldwide — daily in Israel, on holidays in the diaspora.
problem: Not every service: it is said in the morning service (and Musaf), not at every prayer. And 'holidays in the diaspora' is the Ashkenazi practice; most Sephardic communities recite it daily everywhere.
evidence: Wikipedia, Priestly Blessing: 'In Israel, the blessing occurs daily during Shacharit'; 'Ashkenazi Orthodox communities in the diaspora perform it only on holidays'; 'Most Sephardic communities worldwide recite it daily.' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priestly_Blessing
fix: The Priestly Blessing is recited by kohanim (priestly descendants) in synagogue: daily in Israel and in most Sephardic communities, and only on festivals in Ashkenazi communities outside Israel.

current: The Talmud specifies that it must be chanted with joy, not grudgingly, and that kohanim must wash their hands (duchening) before ascending to bless.
problem: The Talmud's blessing says 'with love', not 'with joy' (the 'with joy' ruling is the Rema's, per the source). 'Duchening' means the blessing itself, from dukhan (platform), not the hand-washing.
evidence: Sotah 39a: 'Who has sanctified us with the sanctity of Aaron and commanded us to bless His people, Israel, with love'; 'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says: Any priest who did not first wash his hands may not lift his hands to recite the Priestly Benediction' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Sotah.39a ; Wikipedia, Priestly Blessing: duchening from 'dukhan – platform' https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priestly_Blessing
fix: The Talmud (Sotah 39a) gives the kohanim a blessing to say first, ending 'to bless His people Israel with love,' and rules that a kohen who has not washed his hands may not bless.

current: During the Amida prayer, the congregation covers their faces with their tallitot, as the blessing is considered a moment of concentrated divine presence.
problem: It is the kohanim who cover their heads with their tallitot; the congregation's custom is not to look at the kohanim's hands. The stated reason is unsourced.
evidence: Wikipedia, Priestly Blessing: Kohanim 'cover their heads with their tallitot,' and congregants traditionally avoid looking at their hands https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priestly_Blessing
fix: During the repetition of the Amida, the kohanim cover their heads with their tallitot, and the congregation's custom is not to look at them.

current: Parents bless their children with the Priestly Blessing every Friday night at the Shabbat table.
problem: A widespread custom stated as universal.
evidence: Wikipedia, Priestly Blessing: 'Jewish parents use the Priestly Blessing text to bless children before Shabbat meals' (custom) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Priestly_Blessing
fix: Many parents bless their children with the Priestly Blessing on Friday night at the Shabbat table.

current: The Nazirite vow, though largely obsolete today, became the model for various Jewish ascetic traditions and remains a legally recognized category in halakha.
problem: No source found that the Nazirite vow was 'the model' for Jewish ascetic traditions.
evidence: No supporting source found; Numbers 6:1-21 defines the vow https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.6.1-21
fix: The Nazirite vow is rare today but remains a category in Jewish law.

current: The Sotah water ordeal has no direct parallel in other ancient Near Eastern law, though water ordeals appear in Mesopotamian legal practice (the Code of Hammurabi prescribes an ordeal by river for certain accusations).
problem: The Hammurabi law in question is itself about a wife suspected of adultery, so it is a close parallel, not just an ordeal for 'certain accusations'.
evidence: Code of Hammurabi §132 (King trans., Avalon): 'If the "finger is pointed" at a man's wife about another man, but she is not caught sleeping with the other man, she shall jump into the river for her husband.' https://avalon.law.yale.edu/ancient/hamcode.asp
fix: The closest ancient parallel is in the Code of Hammurabi (law 132), which says a wife suspected of adultery but not caught must undergo an ordeal by the river.

current: Second-Temple-era texts from Qumran and later rabbinic sources show that the Sotah ritual was actually practiced during the Temple period, administered by the priests in Jerusalem, before being formally suspended by Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai after the Temple's destruction.
problem: The Mishnah says Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai stopped the bitter waters because adulterers became many; it does not place this after the Temple's destruction. No Qumran text was found showing the ritual was practiced.
evidence: Mishnah Sotah 9:9: 'מִשֶּׁרַבּוּ הַמְנָאֲפִים, פָּסְקוּ הַמַּיִם הַמָּרִים, וְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי הִפְסִיקָן' ('From the time when adulterers proliferated, ... the bitter waters [ceased]. And it was Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai who nullified it') https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Mishnah_Sotah.9.9
fix: The Mishnah (Sotah 9:9) says the ritual of the bitter waters stopped when adulterers became many, and that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai put an end to it.

current: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses; Miriam is struck with tzara'at and then healed.
problem: The Torah says Miriam was shut out of the camp seven days and then readmitted; it does not state the healing outright.
evidence: Numbers 12:15 (JPS): 'So Miriam was shut out of camp seven days; and the people did not march on until Miriam was readmitted.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.12.13-15
fix: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses; Miriam is struck with tzara'at, shut out of the camp for seven days, and then brought back.

current: She is healed after seven days of quarantine, the whole camp waiting for her.
problem: The text says she was shut out seven days and readmitted, not that she was healed.
evidence: Numbers 12:15 (JPS): 'So Miriam was shut out of camp seven days; and the people did not march on until Miriam was readmitted.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.12.13-15
fix: She is shut out of the camp for seven days, and the people do not march on until she is brought back.

current: When two young men, Eldad and Medad, prophesy independently in the camp rather than at the tent of meeting, Joshua urgently tells Moses to stop them.
problem: Eldad and Medad were among the seventy elders recorded; the 'young man' (na'ar) is the one who ran to tell Moses.
evidence: Numbers 11:26-27 (JPS): 'Two of the men, one named Eldad and the other Medad, had remained in camp ... they were among those recorded ... An assistant [Or "youth"] ran out and told Moses' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.11.26-27
fix: When two of the elders, Eldad and Medad, prophesy in the camp rather than at the Tent of Meeting, Joshua urgently tells Moses to stop them.

current: This verse became a touchstone for mystical and pietist movements throughout Jewish history.
problem: No source found for this claim.
evidence: No supporting source found.
fix: Cut this sentence.

current: The portion's account of Moses's breaking point — 'I cannot carry this people alone' — is read by the rabbis as a model of authentic human leadership: Moses does not pretend to be invulnerable, and his complaint leads God to create a collaborative governance structure (the seventy elders) rather than dismissing him.
problem: No rabbinic source was found for this reading; it is a modern interpretation attributed to 'the rabbis'. The verse itself supports that God's answer was elders to share the burden.
evidence: Numbers 11:17 (JPS): 'they shall share the burden of the people with you, and you shall not bear it alone.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.11.16-17
fix: When Moses says he cannot carry this people alone, God answers by having seventy elders share the burden with him (Numbers 11:17).

current: The 'passing of spirit' from Moses to the seventy elders is seen in Jewish tradition as the origin of the Sanhedrin — the seventy-one-member supreme religious-legal council that governed Jewish life through the Second Temple period.
problem: The Mishnah derives the Sanhedrin's size from the seventy elders plus Moses (from the verse about gathering them, not the passing of spirit), and the claim that it 'governed Jewish life through the Second Temple period' is a contested historical claim stated as fact.
evidence: Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6: 'The Great Sanhedrin was composed of seventy-one judges ... As it is stated: "Gather Me seventy men of the Elders of Israel" (Numbers 11:16), and together with Moses at the head of this body, there are a total of seventy-one.' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Mishnah_Sanhedrin.1.6
fix: The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 1:6) learns from this passage that the Great Sanhedrin, the supreme court, had seventy-one judges: the seventy elders plus Moses.

current: Miriam's challenge to Moses ('has God only spoken through Moses? Has he not spoken through us too?') raised a genuine theological question about prophetic hierarchy that the Torah answers but the tradition has returned to repeatedly.
problem: The Torah gives these words to Miriam and Aaron together, not Miriam alone. 'The tradition has returned to repeatedly' is unsourced.
evidence: Numbers 12:1-2 (JPS): 'Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses ... They said, "Has GOD spoken only through Moses—and not through us as well?"' https://www.sefaria.org/api/v3/texts/Numbers.12.1-2
fix: Miriam and Aaron's challenge to Moses ('Has God spoken only through Moses—and not through us as well?') raises a question about prophetic rank that the Torah answers in the next verses.
